A barrier at a car park and a roll-up door at a loading dock are the two machines most people walk past every day without thinking of them as machines. Both are a motor between two limit switches, which is a morning’s work. What makes them worth a chapter is the same thing that made the traffic light worth one: everything around the motor. Each moves a heavy thing across a place where people and vehicles go, so each has to know when something is in the way, and each has to do something better than stop when it finds out. both are in Logix Connect as classic scenes, under File → New Project, each opening with its guided track and its own machine faults.

The parking entry gate

The machine

Cars arrive by themselves (Cars per minute), queue, and the first one stops at the kiosk with its wheels on the arming loop. The driver presses for a ticket a second later, takes it a second after it appears, and waits for the boom to be all the way up before driving in. On the closing loop past the boom the car is through; in the garage it takes a stall. The garage has four floors of 24 stalls, 96 in all, and fills from the street up: LEVEL 1, LEVEL 2, LEVEL 3, then the ROOF, the only floor you see from above. Parked cars leave by the exit lane at random (Seconds between cars leaving), over the exit loop, with no barrier. The boom is a motor between two limit switches: 2.4 s for its 90 degrees. Lowered onto a car it rests on the roof, and that is logged and counted. Driven against its stop (or a roof) for four seconds, the motor’s thermal trips and it will not run for twenty. Turn on Some drivers tailgate and a few drivers will drive straight under a raised boom without a ticket, which is the problem every car park has.

The attendant’s controls are where an attendant would find them: on the wall of the booth, in a grey steel station with an engraved nameplate and 22 mm operators in chrome bezels, a black legend plate under each. The key switch is the scene’s Mode_Sel (AUTO or OPEN), RAISE, LOWER and RESET are Raise_PB, Lower_PB and Reset_PB, the red pilot light is Lamp_Fault, and the IN GARAGE counter shows Lot_Count. Click them in the inset and the program sees exactly what it would from the console devices, because they are the same devices.

Every scene has three views now, and they are the same machine: the side view is not a picture of the gate but the gate drawn from the side, so every x in it is the x of the plan, the loops light in the pavement when the plan lights them, and the control station works from either view.

Day and night

The car park runs through the day and the night on the run’s own clock. Day length is how many minutes of run time make a whole 24-hour day: 24 by default, so twelve minutes of daylight, then twelve of night, with a dusk and a dawn between; Start hour sets the clock when the run starts (07:00). A clock beside the counts shows the time. The clock is the recorder’s time, so scrubbing back through a run shows the light as it was. Nothing in the program depends on it: the loops, the eye and the limits work the same in the dark, which is the point. What changes is what you can see, and that is what a night shift on a real gate is like.

Try it: dusk at the kiosk

Set Start hour to 17 and watch dusk come down over the queue at the kiosk, in the plan, the side view and 3D. Then set Day length to 4 and watch a whole day go by in four minutes: the counts and the program do not care.

Watch for: a full floor is not a full garage

The SPACES sign and the LED headers count the cars on each floor; the program knows only Lot_Count against Lot_Capacity. LEVEL 1 FULL with 72 stalls free upstairs is a sign for drivers, not a reason to stop selling tickets.

The program’s index

Exercise 1: a ticket for a car

Three conditions sell a ticket: a car on the arming loop, nobody already being let in, room in the lot. The press makes a one-shot, the one-shot latches a half-second dispense pulse, and the driver taking the ticket latches Open_Req: this car may go. The arming loop in the press rung is the whole point of an arming loop: a ticket handed to somebody walking past is a free car later.

Exercise 2: up for the car, down behind it

The boom goes up while Open_Req is set, to its up limit. The car is through when it stands on the closing loop; when it has left the loop and the eye, Open_Req drops and the boom comes straight down behind it, before the next car can follow it in. The lower rung has the two contacts that keep a boom off a car: the eye just past the arm and the closing loop. A watchdog times the motor: a stroke takes 2.4 s, so a motor still running at 4 s has a limit switch that did not make, and the program drops it before its own thermal does.

Exercise 3: count in, count out

The count goes up on the closing loop and not on the ticket, because a car that comes in without one (an attendant’s Raise, a tailgater) still takes a stall. It is a DINT, not a counter instruction, and it is not cleared at power-up: the cars are still in the lot when the power comes back.

Exercise 4: the lamps

Machine faults on the parking gate

Tools → Inject Machine Fault… lists the faults that belong to the parts on this floor. Each has a fault card: the symptom, what to watch in the I/O to confirm it, the repair, and what a program should do about it. Repair on an active fault removes its cause the way a technician would; whether the machine runs again is up to the program. The reference catches the dead up limit (its watchdog) and flags the blocked eye after 30 s; the dead closing loop and the ticket jam are yours to catch.

Guided: the parking gate

The scene opens with its guided track: Init, Ticket (a car presses and gets one), Boom (up for it, down behind it), Count, Lamps and Ready, with the reference rungs hints first. The boom is a lesson after the ticket on purpose: the first car sits at the kiosk with its ticket in its hand until you write the rung that lets it in.

The roll-up door

The machine

The curtain runs on an operator between an up and a down limit, seven seconds for the full height. A forklift drives out through the door every so often, loads on the dock and comes back; it waits on the floor loop on either side until the door is fully open, honks if it waits half a minute, and once it starts through it keeps going. The door coming down onto its mast (or onto a pallet left in the doorway: click the doorway) rests on it with the safety edge pressed and stops there, because a curtain cannot go through a forklift. Kept driving down, that is a hit. Driven against a stop for four seconds, the operator’s thermal trips.

SignalMeaning
Door_Up inputUp limit switch: the door is fully open
Door_Down inputDown limit switch: the door is fully closed
Eye inputPhoto-eye across the opening, inside face: 1 while the beam is blocked
Edge inputSafety edge on the curtain’s bottom bar: 1 while it is pressed against something
SignalMeaning
Inside_Loop inputA forklift waits on the floor loop inside the door
Outside_Loop inputA forklift waits on the loop outside the door
Door_Pos outputDoor position from the encoder on the operator: 0 shut to 100 fully open (%)
Motor_Up outputDoor operator: open
Motor_Down outputDoor operator: close
Beacon outputAmber warning beacon over the door

The program’s index

Exercise 1: the commands

Two latched commands, open and close, each cancelling the other, so the door always knows which way it was last told to go. Open comes from the button or from a forklift on either loop, and it wins: it is the safe direction. Close comes from the button or the auto-close, never into a blocked eye. Stop, wired normally closed, drops both. The limits end them.

Exercise 2: the motor

Exercise 3: reverse, and the watchdog

This is the routine the door is for. Anything in the doorway while the door is coming down sends it back to fully open: the eye sees it before the curtain gets there, the edge feels it if it does. Not stop: reverse. A door that stops on a forklift’s mast is still on the mast, and the driver cannot back out from under it.

Beyond the classic exercise: position, half open, maintenance

The classic door has two limit switches and three buttons. A real dock door has a little more, and so does this one. The two limit switches are drawn as what they are: roller-lever switches on brackets on the guide, LS1 at the top and LS2 at the floor, each tripped by a striker on the curtain’s bottom bar and each with a bright LED that is lit while it is made. They are the only things that tell the program where the door is, unless the operator also has an encoder: this one does, and Door_Pos says 0 shut to 100 fully open. With it the station has a HALF OPEN button (half way, for air or a person on foot, with no switch at half way: the door stops on a LIM window around 50 %, because it moves 0.7 % a scan and an EQU could be stepped over) and a position display in colour bands. A RUN / MAINT key turns the buttons into hold-to-run, the way a technician wants them while adjusting the door: nothing latches, the door moves while the button is held, and the safety edge still stops it. And two sensors that measure the same thing are worth comparing: a limit switch made with Door_Pos nowhere near it means one of them is lying, which the program treats as a fault.

Exercise 4: the beacon and the lamps

Machine faults on the roll-up door

Tools → Inject Machine Fault… lists the faults that belong to the parts on this floor. Each has a fault card: the symptom, what to watch in the I/O to confirm it, the repair, and what a program should do about it. Repair on an active fault removes its cause the way a technician would; whether the machine runs again is up to the program. The reference’s watchdog catches the dead up limit and the broken chain; the stuck edge makes it reverse every close, which keeps everybody safe and the door open, and the exercise is to tell an edge fault from an obstruction.

Guided: the roll-up door

The scene opens with its guided track: Init, Commands, Motor (fully open, fully closed), Safety (close it onto a pallet and it reverses), Lamps and Ready. The forklift runs throughout, so from the Commands lesson on it asks for the door every half a minute: the loops in the open rung are what answer it.

Try it: one program, both machines

The two programs have the same skeleton: a latched request, a motor between two limits interlocked against itself, something that must never be under the moving part, a watchdog. Write the boom’s logic again in the shape of the door’s (an Open_Cmd and a Close_Cmd, a reverse on the eye and the closing loop) and compare. Which one would you rather troubleshoot at two in the morning?

rungs.head: Rung 0
rungs.comment: THE INDEX. Init on the first scan; then every scan: the ticket, the boom, the counts, the lamps
rungs.words: When S:FS is on, the rung runs the routine Init.
rungs.ltr:
1. XIC(S:FS) Examine If Closed asks: true when S:FS is on.
  2. JSR(Init) Jump to Subroutine does: runs the routine Init. The routine is scanned at this point, then the scan comes back here.

pats.t: Part of the index: one call, one job.
pats.why: The main routine calls each routine in turn. A routine that is not called is not scanned, however correct its rungs are.
pats.think: a running order on a clipboard: the main routine reads it top to bottom, and each line sends you to a page that does one job.
pats.watch: A new routine does nothing until a JSR calls it. If a routine’s rungs never highlight online, look here first.

rungs.head: Init · Rung 0
rungs.comment: FIRST SCAN: no car is being let in, no ticket is half dispensed, no fault. Lot_Count is not cleared: the cars in the lot are still there after a power blink

pred.q: S:FS is on. What does the rung do?
pred.a: The rung is true: Open_Req is unlatched, Car_Thru is unlatched, Vend is unlatched, Gate_Fault is unlatched and Lot_Capacity is written.

rungs.words: When S:FS is on, the rung unlatches Open_Req (This car may go: latched when its ticket is taken (or by Raise), dropped when it is through), unlatches Car_Thru (The car being let in has reached the closing loop), unlatches Vend (A ticket is being dispensed), unlatches Gate_Fault (The boom motor ran too long: a limit switch or the motor has failed. Reset clears it) and puts 90 into Lot_Capacity (Stalls in the garage (90: 18 on LEVEL 1, 24 on each floor above)).
rungs.ltr:
1. XIC(S:FS) Examine If Closed asks: true when S:FS is on.
  2. A branch of 5 parallel paths: each path is tested on its own and does its own work.
    Path 1
    1. OTU(Open_Req) Output Unlatch does: unlatches Open_Req. It only ever clears the bit.
    Path 2
    1. OTU(Car_Thru) Output Unlatch does: unlatches Car_Thru. It only ever clears the bit.
    Path 3
    1. OTU(Vend) Output Unlatch does: unlatches Vend. It only ever clears the bit.
    Path 4
    1. OTU(Gate_Fault) Output Unlatch does: unlatches Gate_Fault. It only ever clears the bit.
    Path 5
    1. MOV(90,Lot_Capacity) Move does: puts 90 into Lot_Capacity. It writes every scan the rung is true.

pats.t: An unlatch.
pats.why: This rung is the other half of a latch: it clears Open_Req when its conditions are met, and does nothing otherwise.

rungs.head: Ticket · Rung 0
rungs.comment: THE KIOSK. PRESS FOR TICKET lights only with a car on the arming loop, nobody already being let in, and room in the lot

pred.q: Arming_Loop is on, Open_Req is on and Full is off. What does the rung do?
pred.a: The rung is false: Ticket_Lamp is off. It stops at XIO(Open_Req).

rungs.words: When Arming_Loop (Gate Arming_Loop: A car stands over the loop at the ticket kiosk) is on, Open_Req (This car may go: latched when its ticket is taken (or by Raise), dropped when it is through) is off and Full (The lot is full) is off, the rung turns Ticket_Lamp (Gate Ticket_Lamp: PRESS FOR TICKET lamp on the kiosk) on (and off whenever the rung is false).
rungs.ltr:
1. XIC(Arming_Loop) Examine If Closed asks: true when Arming_Loop is on.
  2. XIO(Open_Req) Examine If Open asks: true when Open_Req is off.
  3. XIO(Full) Examine If Open asks: true when Full is off.
  4. OTE(Ticket_Lamp) Output Energize does: turns Ticket_Lamp on (and off whenever the rung is false). Every scan it writes the rung state: true on, false off.

rungs.head: Ticket · Rung 1
rungs.comment: The press, with a car there: one ticket per press. No car on the loop, no ticket: a ticket handed to a pedestrian is a free car later
rungs.words: When Arming_Loop (Gate Arming_Loop: A car stands over the loop at the ticket kiosk) is on, Ticket_PB (Gate Ticket_PB: The kiosk's PRESS FOR TICKET button, 1 while pressed) is on, Open_Req (This car may go: latched when its ticket is taken (or by Raise), dropped when it is through) is off, Full (The lot is full) is off and this is the first scan of it, the rung latches Vend (A ticket is being dispensed) on.
rungs.ltr:
1. XIC(Arming_Loop) Examine If Closed asks: true when Arming_Loop is on.
  2. XIC(Ticket_PB) Examine If Closed asks: true when Ticket_PB is on.
  3. XIO(Open_Req) Examine If Open asks: true when Open_Req is off.
  4. XIO(Full) Examine If Open asks: true when Full is off.
  5. ONS(PB_ONS) One Shot asks: true on the first scan its input is true (remembered in PB_ONS). It passes power for one scan only, the scan its input goes from false to true; its storage bit remembers last scan.
  6. OTL(Vend) Output Latch does: latches Vend on. It only ever sets the bit; the bit stays on after the rung goes false.

pats.t: A latch.
pats.why: Vend stays on after this rung goes false; only an OTU somewhere else turns it off. Read the program for that OTU before you trust the bit.
pats.think: a light switch rather than a doorbell: flick it on and it stays on until someone flicks it off.
pats.watch: A latched bit survives a stop, and it survives a download that keeps tag values. If nothing ever unlatches it, the machine remembers a state that is long gone.

pats.t: One-shot: once per event, not once per scan.
pats.why: The rung after the one-shot is true for exactly one scan each time its conditions become true, so what follows happens once per event rather than every 20 ms while the condition lasts.
pats.think: a turnstile. However long you stand in it, it counts you once.
pats.watch: Each one-shot needs its own storage bit. Two one-shots sharing a bit fight over it, and one of them never fires.

rungs.head: Ticket · Rung 2
rungs.comment: The dispense pulse: half a second

pred.q: Vend is on. What does the rung do?
pred.a: The rung is true: T_Vend times toward its preset.

rungs.words: When Vend (A ticket is being dispensed) is on, the rung runs the timer T_Vend (The dispense pulse, half a second) toward 500 ms.
rungs.ltr:
1. XIC(Vend) Examine If Closed asks: true when Vend is on.
  2. TON(T_Vend,500,0) Timer On Delay does: runs the timer T_Vend toward 500 ms. The accumulator counts while the rung is true; .DN comes on at the preset; the moment the rung goes false the timer resets.

pats.t: A timer: it times only while this rung is true.
pats.why: T_Vend counts while the rung is true; its .DN comes on at the preset, and the moment the rung goes false it is back at zero. Other rungs read .DN (or .ACC) to act on the time.
pats.think: a kitchen timer you have to keep holding down. Let go and it springs back to zero.
pats.watch: A rung that resets its own timer’s condition (a timer that cuts its own rung with its .DN) restarts every preset: that is a pulse generator, not a delay. Make sure that is what you meant.

rungs.words: When either (Door_Up (Door Door_Up: Up limit switch: the door is fully open) is on and Door_Pos (Door Door_Pos: Door position from the encoder on the operator: 0 shut to 100 fully open (%)) is less than 90) or (Door_Down (Door Door_Down: Down limit switch: the door is fully closed) is on and Door_Pos is greater than 10), the rung runs the timer T_Enc (A limit made with Door_Pos far from it for 1 s: the encoder or the limit has failed) toward 1000 ms (1 s).
rungs.ltr:
1. A branch of 2 parallel paths: power gets through if any one of them is true.
    Path 1
    1. XIC(Door_Up) Examine If Closed asks: true when Door_Up is on.
    2. LES(Door_Pos,90) Less Than asks: true when Door_Pos is less than 90.
    Path 2
    1. XIC(Door_Down) Examine If Closed asks: true when Door_Down is on.
    2. GRT(Door_Pos,10) Greater Than asks: true when Door_Pos is greater than 10.
  2. TON(T_Enc,1000,0) Timer On Delay does: runs the timer T_Enc toward 1000 ms (1 s). The accumulator counts while the rung is true; .DN comes on at the preset; the moment the rung goes false the timer resets.

pats.t: A timer: it times only while this rung is true.
pats.why: T_Enc counts while the rung is true; its .DN comes on at the preset, and the moment the rung goes false it is back at zero. Other rungs read .DN (or .ACC) to act on the time.

pats.t: A window, not a value.
pats.why: A moving value can step over any single number between two scans; a window catches it on the way through.

rungs.head: Safety · Rung 6

pred.q: T_Enc.DN is on. What does the rung do?
pred.a: The rung is true: Door_Fault latches on, Open_Cmd is unlatched, Close_Cmd is unlatched and Half_Cmd is unlatched.

rungs.words: When T_Enc.DN (the done bit of T_Enc: A limit made with Door_Pos far from it for 1 s: the encoder or the limit has failed) is on, the rung latches Door_Fault (The motor ran too long: a limit switch, the chain or the motor has failed. Reset clears it) on, unlatches Open_Cmd (Open the door: latched by Open, a forklift on a loop, or a reversal; dropped at the up limit), unlatches Close_Cmd (Close the door: latched by Close or the auto-close; dropped at the down limit or by a reversal) and unlatches Half_Cmd (Go to half open: latched by HALF, dropped inside 48..52 % of Door_Pos).
rungs.ltr:
1. XIC(T_Enc.DN) Examine If Closed asks: true when T_Enc.DN is on.
  2. A branch of 4 parallel paths: each path is tested on its own and does its own work.
    Path 1
    1. OTL(Door_Fault) Output Latch does: latches Door_Fault on. It only ever sets the bit; the bit stays on after the rung goes false.
    Path 2
    1. OTU(Open_Cmd) Output Unlatch does: unlatches Open_Cmd. It only ever clears the bit.
    Path 3
    1. OTU(Close_Cmd) Output Unlatch does: unlatches Close_Cmd. It only ever clears the bit.
    Path 4
    1. OTU(Half_Cmd) Output Unlatch does: unlatches Half_Cmd. It only ever clears the bit.

pats.t: A latch.
pats.why: Door_Fault stays on after this rung goes false; only an OTU somewhere else turns it off. Read the program for that OTU before you trust the bit.

rungs.head: Safety · Rung 7
rungs.comment: Count the openings (maintenance counts cycles: springs and cables have a life)
rungs.words: When Door_Up (Door Door_Up: Up limit switch: the door is fully open) is on and this is the first scan of it, the rung makes Open_Count (Times the door has opened) = Open_Count + 1.
rungs.ltr:
1. XIC(Door_Up) Examine If Closed asks: true when Door_Up is on.
  2. ONS(Up_ONS) One Shot asks: true on the first scan its input is true (remembered in Up_ONS). It passes power for one scan only, the scan its input goes from false to true; its storage bit remembers last scan.
  3. ADD(Open_Count,1,Open_Count) Add does: makes Open_Count = Open_Count + 1. Every scan the rung is true; behind a one-shot it adds once per event.

pats.t: One-shot: once per event, not once per scan.
pats.why: The rung after the one-shot is true for exactly one scan each time its conditions become true, so what follows happens once per event rather than every 20 ms while the condition lasts.
